newsitem.title: USA: The bulls are back in town ... or just passing through?.
newsitem.headline: The bulls are back in town ... or just passing through?.

text.p: The bulls are back in town.
After being counted out, stocks are roaring back on cheery earnings and economic reports but the market may still not be out of the woods.
Future earnings are expected to be a big problem that could take some of the euphoria out of the market's rebound.

A buying frenzy in stocks this week propelled the Dow Jones industrial average 173 points higher on Tuesday -- its second biggest single-day gain ever. It was the steepest one-day rise since two days after the "Black Monday" stock market crash of Oct. 19, 1987, when the 30-stock Dow crumbled 508 points.
On Friday, the blue-chip index jumped 94.72 points to 7,071.20, within striking distance of its record 7,085.16 set on March 11. For the week, it rose 332.33 points, the biggest weekly gain ever.
The mood change on Wall Street has been dramatic and it showed that after all is said and done, the stock market can do a good job of discounting things.
The market can be hysterically erratic in the near-term as it reacts to worst-case scenarios, but in the end it will prove to be rational.
After zooming to a record high in mid-March, the Dow index had one of its biggest fall as the psychology turned extremely bearish.

In fact, the negative mentality was the most rampant since the 1990 Gulf War as investors reeled from the Federal Reserve's decision in late March to jack up interest rates by a quarter-percentage-point -- the first rate hike in two years.
The Fed's move also coincided with the start of the earnings reporting season, when the market's anxiety level typically reaches a high pitch.
The market's vibrant comeback has nearly wiped out all of the bad memories from the sell-off between March 12 and April 11 that sliced 700 points off of the world's most closely watched stock index.
Investors are now facing a tough choice of whether to stay on the sidelines or jump back in with both feet.
By the end of the week, the big question was still unanswered: Is this just a teaser rally or the real thing?
The market may not have started on its next bullish phase, some experts say.
"We've made up the ground that was lost in March and April," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst for Prudential Securities.
The high price of stocks is a problem that is still dogging the market, even as the Dow has recovered to within proximity of its all-time high.

"The stock market has returned to the level where it had trouble the last time, and we are likely to see the Dow's rise stall because of concern over future earnings," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer for First Albany Corp. in Albany, N.Y.
"I don't see a new round of, 'We're off to the races', because of the high valuation of stocks, particularly the large stocks which are pretty pricey," he said.

"We've been here before and people expect that the growth rate of earnings is going to slow in each of the next four quarters and the market will not get the kick from really exciting earnings," he said.
This week's batch of economic reports confirmed that the economy was growing at a nice pace and inflation was still very in check.
The unemployment rate fell in April to 4.9 percent, its lowest in nearly a quarter century, but the good news was that average hourly wages were down 1 cent after rising 5 cents in March.

There has been little wage-driven inflation, despite tightness in the job market. Wall Street has focused on wages because of the Fed's often stated concern that rising wage demands would spark inflation.

Another report this week laid to rest fears of wage-led inflation as the government said that its Employment Cost Index rose only 0.6 percent in the first quarter from 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter.
News late Friday of a pact between the White House and congressional Republican leaders on a plan to balance the federal budget gave the market an added boost.
Earnings also cooperated.

According to I.B.E.S., a firm that tracks analysts' earnings expectations, out of 416 companies in the Standard & Poor's 500 index that reported quarterly earnings as of Friday, 60 percent had positive results, while only 23 percent posted disappointing earnings. Sixteen percent were on target with analysts' forecasts.

The stock market's rally also confirmed that the recent sell-off was only a correction in a bull market. The price fall fit the profile of a correction as the Dow lost about 10 percent, instead of 20 percent in a more serious bear market.
The Nasdaq composite index jumped 34.83 points Friday to 1,305.33, and was up 96.04 on the week.

The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks gained 14.44 points to 812.97, a gain of 47.60 on the week. The American Stock Exchange index soared 10.00 to 568.50, and stood 25.67 points higher from last Friday.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks gained 7.26 to 422.97, and was up 22.59 for the week.
